title: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, ‘I have done no wrong.’”
paragraphs: “Such is the way of an adulterous woman: she eats, wipes her mouth, and says, ‘I have done no wrong.’”
Read it again.
Slowly.
She eats.
She wipes.
She denies.
The picture is almost shockingly ordinary.
Someone finishes a meal, wipes away the evidence, gets up from the table, and continues with life.
Nothing to see here.
Nothing happened.
And that is precisely the horror of the image.
Sin has become ordinary enough to consume without trembling and convenient enough to erase without repentance.
The Hebrew calls her אִשָּׁה מְנָאָפֶת — ishah mena’afet, an adulterous woman.
And after the act she says:
לֹא־פָעַלְתִּי אָוֶן — lo-fa’alti aven.
“I have done no wrong.”
That sentence may be more dangerous than the scandal itself.
Because there is hope for the sinner who falls to the floor crying, “God, be merciful to me.”
There is hope for the prodigal who finally realizes the pigpen is not home.
There is hope for Peter weeping bitterly after denying Jesus.
There is hope for the person whose hands are dirty but whose heart finally stops pretending they are clean.
But what happens when we become so comfortable with darkness that we stop calling it darkness?
What happens when conviction arrives and we immediately wipe our mouth?
“I deserve to be happy.”
“God understands.”
“Everybody does it.”
“It wasn't technically adultery.”
“We never slept together.”
“It was just messaging.”
“My marriage was already dead.”
“I only looked.”
“I can stop whenever I want.”
“At least I'm not as bad as them.”
“Nobody knows.”
“No one got hurt.”
“I prayed about it.”
And perhaps the most dangerous one:
“God knows my heart.”
Yes.
He does.
That should sober us more than comfort us when we are using grace to protect something Jesus is calling us to surrender.
Because God sees what the spouse does not see.
God sees the deleted conversation.
God sees the second account.
God sees what happens when the browser history disappears.
God sees the emotional affair nobody has named an affair.
God sees the bitterness rehearsed privately.
God sees the secret appetite.
God sees the money nobody knows about.
God sees the private compromise behind the public ministry.
God sees what we keep explaining away.
And this passage is not permission for men to point self-righteously at women.
If you read Proverbs 30:20 merely thinking, “What a terrible woman,” you may have missed the mirror.
The image concerns an adulterous woman, but the spiritual pathology of committing wrong and then denying, minimizing, concealing, or normalizing it belongs to humanity.
Men wipe their mouths too.
Pastors can wipe their mouths.
Church members can wipe their mouths.
Husbands can.
Wives can.
Single people can.
Religious people can become frighteningly skilled at it.
You can sing worship songs on Sunday with lips that spent Saturday destroying somebody in private.
You can post Scripture publicly while feeding an addiction privately.
You can say “God first” in your biography while knowingly placing Him last in your decisions.
You can learn Christian vocabulary without developing Christian repentance.
You can even learn how to use grace as a napkin.
Sin.
Wipe.
Smile.
Repeat.
Until conviction becomes quieter.
But there is something we must make absolutely clear.
The adulterous woman of Proverbs 30:20 should not simply be identified with the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
They are different passages making different points.
Proverbs gives us the chilling picture of someone who says, essentially, “I have done nothing wrong.”
The woman standing before Jesus in John 8 does not say that.
She is standing exposed.
Accused.
Humiliated.
Her sin has become public spectacle.
And there, in one of the Gospel’s most famous scenes, religious men bring a woman caught in adultery before Jesus.
Imagine the sound.
Feet scraping across the ground.
Voices rising.
People staring.
No carefully written testimony.
No polished Sunday clothes capable of hiding what has happened.
Her shame has a crowd.
The accusers have a question.
And Jesus has the final word.
Eventually the accusers leave.
Then comes the exchange that generations of broken people have clung to.
Jesus asks whether anyone has condemned her.
She answers:
Οὐδείς, κύριε — Oudeis, kyrie.
“No one, Lord.”
Then Jesus says:
Οὐδὲ ἐγώ σε κατακρίνω· πορεύου … μηκέτι ἁμάρτανε.
“Neither do I condemn you. Go … sin no more.”
Do not tear that sentence in half.
Our generation desperately needs both sides.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
And:
“Sin no more.”
Grace does not say sin never happened.
Grace says sin does not have to write the final chapter.
Jesus does not stand beside the woman and announce, “Adultery isn't really a problem.”
He does not redefine holiness to protect her feelings.
He does not call evil good.
Yet neither does He join a bloodthirsty crowd eager to reduce a human being to the worst thing associated with her life.
That is what makes Jesus so breathtaking.
Perfect holiness stands in front of human failure...
and holiness does not become compromise.
Mercy does not become permission.
Truth does not become cruelty.
Grace does not become denial.
The Savior neither celebrates sin nor abandons the sinner.
“Neither do I condemn you.”
Grace.
“Go, and sin no more.”
Transformation.
This is where some of us have misunderstood the Gospel.
We thought Jesus came merely to make us feel better about the person we refuse to stop becoming.
But Jesus did not die merely to make sin more emotionally comfortable.
He came to save sinners.
Forgive sinners.
Cleanse sinners.
Reconcile sinners to God.
Give sinners new hearts.
Call sinners out of darkness.
And ultimately transform those who belong to Him.
The Gospel is not Jesus standing beside your chains saying, “Don't feel ashamed about these.”
The Gospel is Jesus paying an unimaginable price to break your chains and then calling you to walk with Him in freedom.
That means there is a difference between conviction and condemnation.
Condemnation whispers:
“You sinned, therefore there is no hope for you.”
The Gospel says:
“You sinned, therefore you desperately need the Savior—and the Savior came for sinners.”
Condemnation tells you to run away from Christ.
Conviction drives you toward Him.
Condemnation says, “Hide.”
Grace says, “Come into the light.”
Condemnation says, “Your scandal is your identity.”
Jesus says something far greater:
Your sin may explain why you need saving.
It does not possess the authority to overrule what Christ can make of a surrendered life.
And maybe that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Maybe your scandal never became public.
Maybe nobody dragged you into the middle of a crowd.
Maybe your husband doesn't know.
Maybe your wife doesn't know.
Maybe your parents don't know.
Maybe your pastor doesn't know.
Maybe the people who follow you online would be shocked.
Maybe you have become so practiced at wiping your mouth that even you barely feel the stain anymore.
But you know.
And God knows.
So here is the question Proverbs 30:20 quietly forces upon us:
What have you been wiping from your mouth while telling yourself you did nothing wrong?
Don't answer quickly.
What have you renamed so you would not have to repent of it?
What have you called “a weakness” that God calls you to put to death?
What relationship have you defended because surrendering it would hurt?
What habit have you hidden because bringing it into the light would cost you something?
What apology have you refused because pride matters more than reconciliation?
What secret have you protected more fiercely than your intimacy with Jesus?
What if the greatest danger facing your soul right now is not that God refuses to forgive you...
but that you have become determined to insist there is nothing requiring forgiveness?
Scripture says:
“If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.”
Then immediately comes hope:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice the difference.
One person says:
Nothing is wrong.
The other says:
God, I have sinned.
One wipes the mouth.
The other opens the heart.
One protects the image.
The other seeks cleansing.
Christianity does not begin with pretending you are clean.
It begins with admitting you cannot cleanse yourself.
That is why the cross matters.
If human beings were basically fine and simply needed encouragement, Calvary would make no sense.
If sin could be removed by self-improvement, the Son of God did not need to shed His blood.
If our deepest problem were low self-esteem, we would need inspiration.
But if our deepest problem is sin separating rebellious humanity from a holy God, we need reconciliation.
We need forgiveness.
We need redemption.
We need Jesus Christ.
At the cross, God does something far greater than pretend our sins never mattered.
Christ bears sin.
Justice is not mocked.
Grace is not cheapened.
Forgiveness is purchased at terrible cost.
The innocent One suffers for the guilty.
And then comes resurrection morning.
The stone moves.
Death loses its claim.
The crucified Christ rises.
And suddenly the Gospel announces something scandalously beautiful:
Your sin can be confessed without becoming your final identity because Jesus Christ is alive.
Peter's denial was not his final chapter.
The thief's criminal past was not his final chapter.
The persecutor Saul's violence was not his final chapter.
And your darkest chapter does not have to be your final chapter either.
But grace is not pretending the chapter was beautiful.
Grace is allowing Jesus to rewrite what sin tried to destroy.
That is the heartbeat of Gospel Warrior:
Not from scandal to denial.
Not from scandal to excuses.
Not from scandal to carefully managed appearances.
From scandal...
to repentance...
to mercy...
to restoration...
to transformation...
through Jesus Christ.
Maybe you have spent years believing repentance means God is waiting to humiliate you.
Look again at Christ.
Repentance is not paying God back.
You cannot.
Repentance is not earning forgiveness.
You cannot.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the God whose mercy you could never deserve and whose Son accomplished what you could never accomplish for yourself.
The Greek word so often associated with repentance in the New Testament, μετάνοια — metanoia, speaks of a change of mind, a turning that reaches into the direction of life.
Biblical repentance is deeper than saying, “Sorry I got caught.”
It is deeper than crying while secretly planning to return.
It is deeper than deleting evidence while preserving desire.
Repentance says:
“Jesus, I agree with You about my sin.”
“No more excuses.”
“No more hiding.”
“No more calling darkness light.”
“I cannot save myself.”
“Have mercy on me.”
“Change me.”
And perhaps someone reading this is thinking:
You don't know what I've done.
You're right.
I don't.
But Jesus does.
Maybe you betrayed someone who trusted you.
Maybe pornography has been consuming years of your life.
Maybe you crossed boundaries you once swore you never would.
Maybe your marriage is bleeding because of choices nobody else understands.
Maybe you have lied so many times that you no longer remember which version of yourself people believe.
Maybe you abandoned God and now feel hypocritical even whispering His name.
Maybe you are reading an article about an adulterous woman while carrying your own secret scandal.
Hear this carefully.
The answer is not:
“I have done nothing wrong.”
And the answer is not:
“I have done too much wrong for Jesus.”
Both statements keep you from grace.
One denies the disease.
The other denies the Physician.
The Gospel destroys both lies.
Yes, sin is real.
Yes, judgment is real.
Yes, repentance matters.
And yes...
Jesus saves sinners.
That includes the ashamed.
The compromised.
The sexually broken.
The religious hypocrite who finally stops pretending.
The prodigal who smells like the far country.
The believer who wandered.
The person who thought they would never fall this far.
Christ's invitation is not permission to remain there.
It is an invitation to come home.
Maybe today is the day you stop wiping your mouth.
Maybe today is the day the secret finally becomes a confession before God.
Maybe today you contact the mature believer or pastor you have been avoiding and say, “I need help.”
Maybe today you remove access to what keeps dragging you backward.
Maybe today you stop negotiating with the thing Christ is telling you to surrender.
Not because surrender purchases God's love.
But because the grace that saves us also teaches us that sin is no longer our master.
And please don't turn this article into ammunition against somebody else's scandal.
Where are you wiping your mouth?
Where am I tempted to excuse what God wants brought into the light?
The ground beneath the cross destroys boasting.
There are no superior sinners standing there.
Only needy people and a sufficient Savior.
So if this exposed something you have been hiding, you don't need to publish the details of your sin in a Facebook comment.
But you can take one small step out of hiding.
Or simply write:
Let those words become more than engagement.
Let them become a line in the sand.
And then actually seek prayer.
Actually confess where appropriate.
Actually pursue accountability.
Actually return to Christ.
If somebody came to your mind while reading this—not someone you want to embarrass, but someone you genuinely love—send this to them privately.
He does.
And He calls them out of darkness.
Go to Jesus.
The point is not Gospel Warrior.
The point is Christ.
The One who sees the stain you tried to wipe away.
The One before whom excuses collapse.
The One who knows the chapter you wish had never been written.
The One who calls sin what it is...
and still stretches wounded hands toward sinners who repent and believe.
You do not need another napkin.
You need cleansing.
You do not need a better excuse.
You need mercy.
You do not need to convince God that nothing happened.
You need to discover that Jesus already knows what happened—and the Gospel is powerful enough to meet repentant sinners there.
So stop wiping your mouth.
Stop rehearsing the defense.
Stop running.
Bring the scandal into the light of Christ.
Because the most unforgettable thing about grace is not that Jesus helps us pretend the stain was never there.
It is that He can take the very life sin tried to ruin and make it a testimony to the mercy of God.
And maybe the sentence you have been afraid to speak—
“Jesus, I sinned. Please forgive me.”
—is the sentence that finally opens the door to the chapter you thought could never be written.
Your scandal may explain how you arrived at Jesus' feet, but it does not get to decide who rises from them.
